hints: Start by separating the two organisms involved - the pathogen that causes malaria and the organism that carries it between people. Which one is the vector?
Think of transmission as two linked blood meals - what the mosquito picks up from an infected person and what it then puts into an uninfected person when it feeds again.
walkthrough:
Name the Correct Vector**
Malaria is not spread by direct contact or in air. The pathogen Plasmodium needs a vector to move from person to person. That vector is the female Anopheles mosquito. Only the female feeds on blood, so only she can transmit.

Link the Two Feeds**
First the mosquito feeds on an infected person and takes up Plasmodium in the blood. Later, when it feeds on an uninfected person, it injects saliva containing anticoagulant to keep blood flowing. Plasmodium in the saliva enters the new person's blood, so infection passes on.

Final answer: Malaria is transmitted by the bite of a female Anopheles mosquito acting as vector. The mosquito takes a blood meal from an infected person and later injects saliva containing Plasmodium parasites into the blood of an uninfected person.

hints: Look at the box after the immune response - which type of white blood cell divides to make antibody-secreting plasma cells?
Look at the middle box where two cell types come together - what word means two cells joining into one combined cell?
Recall the special name given to the combined dividing cell that makes one type of antibody and divides continuously.
walkthrough:
Cells That Make Antibody**
When malarial antigen is injected, the mouse makes an immune response. The specific B-lymphocytes that recognise that antigen divide by clonal selection to form many plasma cells. Plasma cells secrete antibody but cannot divide forever.

Joining With Cancer Cells**
To keep antibody production going, plasma cells from the spleen are fused with myeloma cells. Myeloma is a fast-dividing tumour cell of the same lineage, so the fused cell keeps both properties.

Naming the Product**
The fused cell is called a hybridoma cell. Each hybridoma divides to form a clone that secretes large amounts of one specific monoclonal antibody against the malarial antigen.
Final answer: specific B-lymphocytes / B-cells divide to form many plasma cells; plasma cells fused with myeloma cells; formation of hybridoma cells.

walkthrough:
Fast and Reliable Result**
The strip uses monoclonal antibodies so it is specific and accurate for malarial antigen. You just add blood to S and buffer to A, then read lines at C and T. A result appears in minutes, so diagnosis is quick.

Simple and Cheap in the Field**
The test is cheap, portable and needs only a tiny drop of blood. It needs no microscope, electricity or highly trained worker, and is easy to transport in bulk to remote areas.

Better Treatment Decisions**
Because malaria is confirmed at once, the correct antimalarial can be given immediately. This saves lives and stops giving antimalarial drugs just in case when the person is negative.

Final answer: Any three: results accurate and specific due to monoclonal antibodies; results obtained quickly for rapid diagnosis; cheap / low cost; easy to use and read with no highly trained staff needed; no specialised laboratory equipment needed; easily transported; only small blood sample needed; allows immediate correct treatment and avoids unnecessary use of antimalarial drugs.

walkthrough:
Follow the Vector**
Malaria can only spread where its vector, the Anopheles mosquito, can live. That means tropical warm and humid regions, which is why sub-Saharan Africa and South-East Asia have the most cases.

Warmth for Parasite and Mosquito**
Warm temperatures speed up development of Plasmodium inside the mosquito and growth of mosquito larvae. Humid air helps adult mosquitoes survive long enough to transmit.

Water and Landscape**
Females lay eggs in still water such as ponds, puddles and swamps, so areas with high rainfall have many breeding sites. Low altitude is warmer and wetter than high mountains, so lowlands favour mosquitoes.

Resistance Keeps Malaria High**
Where mosquitoes have evolved insecticide or repellent resistance, spraying and nets work less well. Where Plasmodium has evolved drug resistance, treatment fails, so transmission continues.

People and Prevention**
Distribution is also set by human factors. Poor areas without full control measures like bed nets, indoor spraying and drainage stay high. Movement of infected people brings parasites to new areas, and populations with little immunity or high HIV infection are more vulnerable.

Final answer: Any five: distribution follows distribution of Anopheles vector which needs warm humid tropical climate; warm temperature needed for development of Plasmodium in mosquito and for mosquito larvae; mosquitoes need still water bodies for breeding and sufficient rainfall; humid conditions and low altitude favour mosquitoes; insecticide resistance in mosquitoes and drug resistance in Plasmodium maintain high cases; areas where prevention / control such as nets, spraying, drainage not fully implemented have more malaria; migration of infected people spreads malaria; low immunity and high HIV rates increase cases.
